validator: draft 1 passed with no problems, soft problems or warnings
keep: The idea is named in the first two sentences: a steady net torque makes the speed climb steadily, at a rate set by the moment of inertia, its mass and how far out it sits.

T = I × α is derived, not asserted: one mass on an arm, push T ÷ r, Newton's second law along the circle, speed along the circle ω × r, so the radius counts twice. The rig's numbers follow from it: 2 × 25 × 0.2² = 2 kg m², 25 rad/s², 6.1 s; 8 kg m² and 24.3 s at 0.4 m.
Work = T × θ and P = T × ω come from the arm turning one radian, and ½Iω² from lesson 5's ½mv² with v = ωr, so nothing new is taken on trust. The rad/s rule is footnoted where he would look it up.

Each brief misconception has a DO screen and a wrong pick: steady torque means steady speed (screens 2 and 14), the energy and the moment of inertia (screens 4 and 10, radius and speed not squared), ω not squared (screen 10), and rev/min left unconverted (screens 6, 8 and 13).
The motor and pump switch goes deeper than Motors lesson 4 rather than over it: the same curves, now with the time the inertia takes, and screen 12 asks where the run-up settles.
Fourteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) and end on two mixed puzzles (13, 14), the 14 the brief allows this lesson.
The analogy is from his trade, a steady current into a capacitor: straight-line rise and ½CV² against ½Iω², and its break, the moment of inertia changing with no torque, is correct science.
fix: Causal step skipped: 'So ω rises by T ÷ (m × r²) each second' jumps from the push along the circle to ω. Say that because the speed along the circle is ω × r, ω rises by that gain ÷ r.
False absolute: 'a pump's load torque grows as it speeds up' is not true of every pump. Say a load such as a pump or a fan often needs more torque the faster it turns.

False absolute: 'it turns the shaft without pushing it anywhere' is untrue of a belt drive's pull. Say a motor's own torque acts like the couple in Moments and beams, turning the shaft without pushing it sideways.

Brief shows the effect without its cause: the readouts give speed, run-up time and energy, but not the moment of inertia that makes the run-up four times longer. Make the first readout the moment of inertia in kg m²; the speed reads off the graph.

Check tests recall: screen 8 asks the power of 72.4 N m at 1450 rev/min, the very case screen 7 has just shown backwards. Use a new case, 40 N m at 960 rev/min: 4.02 kW, with wrong picks 38.4 kW (rev/min left in) and 640 W (revolutions a second).
Number clash: the practice worked example's 20 rad/s² and 7.6 s repeat screen 6's wrong pick. Use an example 3 kg m² and 40 N m: 13.3 rad/s², 11.4 s, 34.6 kJ.

Plain writing: 'A longer arm turns the same torque into a smaller push, and the mass must also go faster…' runs to 25 words; split it. 'Work and power follow from Work, energy and power' reads oddly; point back to the winch by name. The steady-speed sentence should name friction with the load.

shape.rule stated in words: yes: the speed rises by the net torque ÷ the moment of inertia each second; I adds m × r² for each mass
shape.one worked example with real numbers: yes: the 2 kg m² rig under 50 N m, and a fan rotor in practice
shape.misconception shown failing: yes: a steady torque raising the speed steadily (screens 1 and 2), a shaft at steady speed with no net torque (screen 14), radius and speed not squared (screens 4 and 10)
shape.analogy with where it breaks: yes: a steady current into a capacitor
